messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean,

Regarding imputing missing values for 'density' as Mathias noted: there are multiple ways to do this. One way is fixing density NA's equal to the mean of the observed density [i, j], and another is treating density [i, j] as a stochastic node: density[i, j]~dnorm(mu.obs.density, tau.obs.density), where mu.obs.density and tau.obs.density are the sample mean and precision of the observed data. The prior distribution for density in option 2 may not necessarily be normal, depending upon what the variable is: e.g., density[i, j]~dpois(lam.obs.density), or even estimating missing values as a function of yet additional covariates, etc.  There are probably several other ways to approach this as well.  Either way, it might be worth assessing sensitivity to different methods of dealing with missing values.

Otherwise, is forest indexed correctly as forest[i,]?  It looks the data are a matrix (forest[i,] vs. forest[i]).

One final thought: my memory is that there were some issues with R2JAGS (incorrect burn-in or something like that). I don't know if this has been fixed, but you might prefer to use 'jagsUI' or 'rjags'.  The former makes the running of chains in parallel very easy, which is a nice feature.

John

messages.subject: incorporating patch existence in dynamic occupancy model
messages.subject_clean: incorporating patch existence in dynamic occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I’m trying to run a dynamic site-occupancy model (cf section 13.5 in Kéry & Schaub 2012), while also incorporating information on whether any given site exists at each of my primary sampling periods. The reason I wish to do this is because throughout my dataset, new sites were introduced (created) each year, plus some have been destroyed over the course of the study.

The processes governing these site creation/removal events are very different biologically to those governing survival/colonisation within the site, and so I’d likely to distinguish between extinction caused by the removal of a patch vs loss of the species within a patch.

Currently, my way of incorporating that has been to create a binary matrix (existence) specifying for each j year, whether each i site existed, and incorporating this as follows:

    muZ[i,k] <- (z[i,k-1]*phi[k-1]*existence[i,k]) + ((1-z[i,k-1])*gamma[k-1]* existence[i,k])

    z[i,k] ~ dbern(muZ[i,k])

Thus z can never be non-zero in years where the site didn’t exist.

However, I’m concerned about the effect of this parameterisation on the behaviour of survival (phi) and colonisation (gamma). My goal is to have no information contributed from sites where the patch is destroyed to survival in that year (i.e, removing a site will inevitable mean it is no longer occupied, but I don’t want this to influence survival). I suspect that currently this is not the case, in which case it would seem that by using this model parameterisation I’m biasing the estimates of colonisation and extinction- the prior distributions for these parameters will provide more information than the data for sites that don’t exist.

Is this the case? And if so, is there a better way of calculating the parameters that I’m after?

Thanks for any advice

Sam

messages.subject: Re: incorporating patch existence in dynamic occupancy model
messages.subject_clean: incorporating patch existence in dynamic occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sam,

The best thing you can do is use some of Marc's simulation code and modify it for your particular situation.  If you can recover the data-generating parameters, then you'll have confidence that your model structure works.

The way you've set up the model, your estimates of survival and colonization probability are population parameters for sites that exist.  If you were to calculate the finite sample proportions of survived sites using the latent states, unconditional on existence, they would be different since some of the sites were eliminated and for those sites survival was deterministically zero.

For example, let's say you had 100 sites and 80 of them were occupied in year 1.  In year 2, 20 of the occupied sites were eliminated and of the remaining 60 occupied sites, 40 of them survived to remain occupied.  The survival probability, phi, would be estimated as 40/60 = 0.67, while the finite-sample proportion calculated from the z latent states would be 40/80 = 0.50.  Obviously that last proportion includes both sites that existed and were eliminated, but the survival probably should not be biased.  Essentially, phi uses a denominator that accounts for site existence.

messages.subject: reformatting multidimensional arrays into 2 dimensions
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

my colleague Jerome Guelat just shared the following nice piece of R code with me:

tab <- array(1:120, dim = c(4, 5, 3, 2))
tablong <- as.data.frame.table(tab)

This shows how we can turn a 4 dimensional array into 2 dimensions, the former of which you may think of as representing detection/nondetection data in a dynamic multispecies occupancy model for instance. In BUGS it is usually better to format the data into a regular multidimensional array (such as 'tab'), because the BUGS model looks neater then: the dimensions of the array provide the information about site, rep, year and species. However, sometimes (especially when you have lots of missing values in such an array and large data sets), you must string out the data into a vector and then throw out the NA's to avoid BUGS from choking. This piece of code is useful for this.

(Of course, there are many other ways to do reformatting of multidimensional data, including the powerful functions in the reshape package, which I, however, never have come to fully understand.)

Best regards  --  Marc

messages.subject: Dail-Madsen model with "staggered entry"
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to use the Dail-Madsen model to analyse data collected by volunteers. It is data where volunteers captured toads and carried them across roads to prevent mortality of toads on the roads. The main question is to test for a trend in abundance (in the unmarked language it would be pcountOpen(… , dynamics=”trend”, …)) . JAGS code for such a model is available in the electronic supplement of the paper by Hostetler and Chandler.

We have data from 153 sites and a period of 30 years (1985 to 2014). However, average length of the time series is only about 9 years. Site-speficif data are for different time periods. That is, for one site we may have data from, say, 1985 to 1995, for another site the data may be from 2000 to 2010. Data for a third site data may be from 1997 to 2002.

The Dail-Madsen model estimates an initial abundance, N[i,1] (where i stands for site i). In my data set this would be N[i,1984]. I think it makes no sense to estimate this abundance because for most sites there is simply no data for the first year (1984) of the data set. Because it is a kind of a “staggered entry” design, I think it would be preferable to estimate a site-specific first year abundance.

Would it be possible to replace N[i,1] with N[i,first] where first is a vector that describes the first year for which data are available? I.e, first = c(1985, 2000, 1997, …).

After estimating first year abundance N[i,1], the following years are estimated using a loop
for (t in 2:T)
I would then replace this with
for (t in (first+1):T)
or perhaps
for (t in (first+1):last)
where “last” is a vector that describes the last year for which data is availave (e.g. last=c(1995, 2010, 2001, …).

Would such a modification of the Dail-Madsen model be ok? Is there some assumption of the Dail-Madsen model that might be violated?

Thanks for your help.
Best, Beni

messages.subject: RE: Dail-Madsen model with "staggered entry"
messages.body_plain:
Dear Beni,

I think that you can do two things to alleviate the computational burden of this notorious model in your case:
(1) You can vectorize your analysis, by stringing out all the counts in a single vector, instead of organising them into a regular, 2-dimensional array. The latter means that all the missing responses will be estimated as well in the MCMC updating, adding unnecessarily to the computational burden. For highly imbalanced data sets in hierarchical models such as occupancy and Nmix models etc., this is always one of the first things that one must do to speed up a model.

(2) However, internally, you will then still estimate a lot of latent variables for every site (i) and every year (t). I think that it might be possible to fit a sort of "conditional" DM model, where conditional means "conditional on the years in which you observe data at a site". This would be similar in spirit to the Cormack-Jolly-Seber model, where survival is modelled conditional upon first capture. You could look up BUGS code for the CJS model to see how one may define a vector of first (and in your case, last) observations and then fit the model only to those periods for a site.

I think that such a version of the DM should work, though it would rest upon the untested assumption that the missing value pattern (i.e., whether there is or there is not any count at a site in a year) is ignorable. Comments welcome especially on the 2nd point.

Kind regards  ---  Marc

messages.subject: Re: Dail-Madsen model with "staggered entry"
messages.body_plain:
I also replied to this, but forgot to reply to all...

Hi Beni,

I think you could do this, but would need to make sure that you use the correct expected value of abundance for the "first data year". If the first data year is after the first year of the study, then the expected value would depend on the expected value of abundance from the previous year(s). For the "trend" model, which is just a model of geometric growth, you could do something like:

EN[i,1] <- lambda[i] # Expected value of abundance in year 1
for(t in 2:first[i]) {
  EN[i,t] <- EN[i,t-1]*gamma[i] # Expected value of abundance in year 2
  }
for(t in first[i]:T) {
  N[i,t] ~ dpois(EN[i,t])
  }

For this particular model, if gamma is constant over time, you could simply use:

EN[i,t] <- lambda[i]*gamma^first[i]

Note, however, that you should get similar results using either the expected values of N or the latent realized values of N (the approach you are trying to avoid), although the variance of the later will be greater. Also note that this is one of those cases where "gamma" is normally called "lambda" in the ecological literature, making things somewhat confusing.

Hope this helps. Let us know how it turns out.

Richard

On Mon, Nov 30, 2015 at 10:14 AM, Kery Marc <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:

> Dear Beni,
>
> I think that you can do two things to alleviate the computational burden of this notorious model in your case:
> (1) You can vectorize your analysis, by stringing out all the counts in a single vector, instead of organising them into a regular, 2-dimensional array. The latter means that all the missing responses will be estimated as well in the MCMC updating, adding unnecessarily to the computational burden. For highly imbalanced data sets in hierarchical models such as occupancy and Nmix models etc., this is always one of the first things that one must do to speed up a model.
>
> (2) However, internally, you will then still estimate a lot of latent variables for every site (i) and every year (t). I think that it might be possible to fit a sort of "conditional" DM model, where conditional means "conditional on the years in which you observe data at a site". This would be similar in spirit to the Cormack-Jolly-Seber model, where survival is modelled conditional upon first capture. You could look up BUGS code for the CJS model to see how one may define a vector of first (and in your case, last) observations and then fit the model only to those periods for a site.
>
> I think that such a version of the DM should work, though it would rest upon the untested assumption that the missing value pattern (i.e., whether there is or there is not any count at a site in a year) is ignorable. Comments welcome especially on the 2nd point.
>

> From: hmec...@googlegroups.com [hmec...@googlegroups.com] on behalf of Benedikt Schmidt [benz.s...@gmx.ch]
> Sent: 30 November 2015 11:59
> To: hmec...@googlegroups.com
> Subject: Dail-Madsen model with "staggered entry"
>
> Dear all,
>
> I would like to use the Dail-Madsen model to analyse data collected by volunteers. It is data where volunteers captured toads and carried them across roads to prevent mortality of toads on the roads. The main question is to test for a trend in abundance (in the unmarked language it would be pcountOpen(… , dynamics=”trend”, …)) . JAGS code for such a model is available in the electronic supplement of the paper by Hostetler and Chandler.
>
> We have data from 153 sites and a period of 30 years (1985 to 2014). However, average length of the time series is only about 9 years. Site-speficif data are for different time periods. That is, for one site we may have data from, say, 1985 to 1995, for another site the data may be from 2000 to 2010. Data for a third site data may be from 1997 to 2002.
>
> The Dail-Madsen model estimates an initial abundance, N[i,1] (where i stands for site i). In my data set this would be N[i,1984]. I think it makes no sense to estimate this abundance because for most sites there is simply no data for the first year (1984) of the data set. Because it is a kind of a “staggered entry” design, I think it would be preferable to estimate a site-specific first year abundance.
>
> Would it be possible to replace N[i,1] with N[i,first] where first is a vector that describes the first year for which data are available? I.e, first = c(1985, 2000, 1997, …).
>
> After estimating first year abundance N[i,1], the following years are estimated using a loop
> for (t in 2:T)
> I would then replace this with
> for (t in (first+1):T)
> or perhaps
> for (t in (first+1):last)
> where “last” is a vector that describes the last year for which data is availave (e.g. last=c(1995, 2010, 2001, …).
>
> Would such a modification of the Dail-Madsen model be ok? Is there some assumption of the Dail-Madsen model that might be violated?
>
> Thanks for your help.
> Best, Beni
